In mathematics, the '''Chang number''' of an irreducible representation of a simple complex [[Lie algebra]] is its dimension modulo 1&nbsp;+&nbsp;''h'', where ''h'' is the [[Coxeter number]]. Chang numbers are named after {{harvtxt|Chang|1982}}, who rediscovered an element of order ''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 found by {{harvtxt|Kac|1981}}.

{{harvtxt|Kac|1981}} showed that there is a unique class of [[regular element (Lie theory)|regular element]]s σ of order ''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, in the complex points of the corresponding [[Chevalley group]]. He showed that the trace of σ on an irreducible representation is &minus;1, 0, or +1, and if ''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 is prime then the trace is congruent to the dimension mod ''h''+1.  This implies that the dimension of an irreducible representation is always &minus;1, 0, or +1 mod&nbsp;''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1  whenever ''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 is prime.

==Examples==
In particular, for the exceptional compact [[Lie group]]s [[G2 (mathematics)|''G''<sub>2</sub>]], F4, E6, E7, and E8 the number ''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1&nbsp;= 7, 13, 13, 19, 31 is always prime, so the Chang number of an irreducible representation is always +1, 0, or &minus;1.

For example, the first few irreducible representations of G2 (with Coxeter number ''h''&nbsp;=&nbsp;6)  have dimensions 1, 7, 14, 27, 64, 77, 182, 189, 273, 286,...
These are congruent to 1, 0, 0, &minus;1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, &minus;1,... mod&nbsp;7 =&nbsp;''h''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1.
